ai.literal: Recompense expects not the duty of benevolence; towards the rain, what does indeed the world return?
ai.translation: Benevolent duty expects no return; after all, what does the world give back to the rain clouds that sustain it?
ai.modern: பிறருக்குச் செய்யும் உதவி கைம்மாறை எதிர்பார்ப்பது இல்லை; உலகிற்கு மழையைத் தரும் மேகத்திற்கு இவ்வுலகம் என்ன கைம்மாறு செய்ய முடியும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the selfless nature of true benevolence. The word 'கடப்பாடு' refers to the duty of helping others, which should be done without expecting any 'கைம்மாறு' (recompense or return-benefit). To illustrate this, the poet asks a rhetorical question: what does the world ('உலகு') ever do in return for the rain ('மாரி')? Just as the rain pours down to sustain life without expecting anything back, a wise person performs acts of benevolence purely as a duty to society.

ai.literal: All the wealth yielded by putting forth effort is for the sake of doing benevolence to worthy people.
ai.translation: All the wealth earned through hard work and effort is meant solely for the purpose of helping deserving people.
ai.modern: முயற்சி செய்து ஈட்டிய செல்வங்கள் அனைத்தும் தகுதியுடையவர்களுக்கு உதவி செய்வதற்காகவே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true purpose of earning wealth. The word 'tāḷ' refers to effort or perseverance, and 'āṟṟi' means putting it into practice to earn a living. While 'vēḷāṇmai' literally means agriculture, in this context of social duty, it means benevolence or helping others. The poet emphasizes that the entire sum of wealth accumulated through one's hard work is not for selfish hoarding, but is meant to be used in service of those who are worthy and in need.

ai.literal: Even in the world of gods and here in this world, to obtain other good things than benevolence is rare.
ai.translation: Both in the world of the gods and in this earthly world, it is difficult to find any other good thing that is better than benevolence.
ai.modern: தேவர் உலகத்திலும் இந்த உலகத்திலும் ஒப்புரவை விட (பிறருக்கு உதவி செய்வதை விட) சிறந்த வேறு நன்மைகளைப் பெறுவது அரிது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of benevolence (oppuravu), which means living in harmony with society and doing one's duty to others. The poet compares this virtue across two realms: the celestial world of the gods (puttēḷ ulakam) and this earthly world (īṇṭu). It asserts that in neither of these worlds can one acquire any good quality or possession that is superior to benevolence. Thus, serving and sharing with society is established as the highest possible good a person can attain.

ai.literal: He who knows what is fitting (benevolence) is the living man; the other person will be placed among the dead.
ai.translation: He who understands and practices what is fitting for social harmony is the one who truly lives; he who does not will be counted among the dead.
ai.modern: உலக நடைமுறைக்கு ஒத்த உதவி செய்து வாழ்பவனே உயிர் வாழ்பவன் ஆவான்; அவ்வாறு செய்யாத மற்றவன் இறந்தவர்களுள் ஒருவனாகவே கருதப்படுவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true life not by physical breath, but by active participation in social benevolence. The word 'ottatu' refers to that which is fitting or agreeable to the world, meaning living in harmony with society through mutual aid. The benevolent person ('aravon') who practices this is the only one who truly lives ('uyirvalvan'). In contrast, the selfish person ('matraiyan') who does not contribute to the community is considered socially and spiritually dead, and is therefore counted among the deceased ('cettarul vaikkappadum').

ai.literal: Like a village drinking-water pond being filled with water is the wealth of a person of great wisdom who is desired by the world.
ai.translation: The wealth of a wise and benevolent person, who is loved by the world, is like a village drinking-water pond filled to the brim, accessible and beneficial to all.
ai.modern: உலகத்தாரால் விரும்பப்படும் பேரறிவாளனின் செல்வம், ஊர் மக்கள் அனைவரும் குடிப்பதற்காக நீர் நிறைந்த குளத்தைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a beautiful analogy to describe the nature of wealth in the hands of a wise, benevolent person. An 'uruni' is a common drinking-water pond in a village, meant for everyone to quench their thirst freely. Just as the water in such a pond is public, clean, and serves the entire community without discrimination, the wealth accumulated by a wise person who loves and is loved by the world is utilized entirely for the welfare of society. The couplet highlights that true wealth is not meant for private hoarding but for public utility, bringing life and sustenance to all.

ai.literal: If wealth reaches with the one who has benevolence, it is indeed like a fruit tree having ripened inside the village.
ai.translation: When wealth comes to a benevolent person who loves to help others, it is like a fruitful tree ripening in the very center of a village.
ai.modern: பிறருக்கு உதவும் நற்பண்பு உடையவனிடம் செல்வம் சேருவது, ஊரின் நடுவே உள்ள பயன் தரும் மரம் பழுத்திருப்பதைப் போன்றது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet compares the wealth of a benevolent person to a fruit-bearing tree in the middle of a village. A fruit tree located inside a village is accessible to everyone, and its fruits can be enjoyed by all without any hindrance. Similarly, when wealth reaches a person who has the quality of benevolence (நயன்), it is not hoarded but is naturally shared to benefit the entire community. The key words 'பயன்மரம்' (fruitful tree) and 'நயனுடையான்' (benevolent person) highlight how true wealth finds its purpose only when it is accessible and useful to others.

ai.literal: Like a tree that becomes an unfailing medicine in all its parts, indeed, is wealth, if it reaches the hands of a person of great nobility.
ai.translation: If wealth reaches the hands of a person of great nobility, it is like a tree whose every part becomes an unfailing medicine.
ai.modern: பெருந்தன்மையானவரிடத்தில் செல்வம் சேர்ந்தால், அது தனது எல்லா உறுப்புகளும் மருந்தாகிப் பயன்படும் மரத்தைப் போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the wealth of a benevolent person to a medicinal tree. A medicinal tree is one whose bark, leaves, root, and fruit all serve as remedies without failing. Similarly, when wealth reaches a person of great nobility, every bit of it is used to alleviate the suffering of others. The word 'tappā' highlights that the tree never fails to heal, just as the noble person's wealth never fails to help those in need.

ai.literal: Even in a time lacking resources, from benevolence they will not shrink, those who have the vision of knowing their duty.
ai.translation: Even in times of destitution, those who possess the clear vision of duty do not shrink from their benevolence to society.
ai.modern: வறுமைக்காலத்திலும், கடமையை உணர்ந்த அறிவுடையவர்கள் பிறருக்கு உதவி செய்யும் ஒப்புரவுப் பண்பிலிருந்து பின்வாங்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that true benevolence is a matter of character and vision, not just material wealth. The phrase 'கடனறி காட்சியவர்' refers to wise individuals who have a clear, deep understanding of their duty to the community. Even during 'இடனில் பருவம்'—a period when they lack personal resources or face poverty—they do not shrink ('ஒல்கார்') from performing acts of social benevolence ('ஒப்புரவு'). Their commitment to helping others remains steadfast regardless of their financial situation.

words.gloss: one who possesses a benevolent nature

ai.literal: A benevolent person becoming poor is the state of being unable to remain quiet without doing the deeds of his nature.
ai.translation: The poverty of a benevolent person is nothing but the painful state of being unable to perform those acts of charity that are natural to him.
ai.modern: பிறருக்கு உதவி செய்யும் பண்புடையவன் வறியவன் ஆவது என்பது, தன் தகுதிக்கு ஏற்பச் செய்ய வேண்டிய உதவிகளைச் செய்ய முடியாமல் தவிக்கும் நிலையே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet beautifully redefines poverty for a generous soul. For a benevolent person (நயனுடையான்), poverty is not the lack of wealth for personal comfort, but rather the inability to perform acts of charity (செயும் நீர செய்யாது). The word 'நீர' refers to deeds that are natural to a kind heart, and 'அமைகலா ஆறு' highlights the restless distress they feel when they are unable to help others. Thus, their true impoverishment is the forced cessation of their benevolence.

ai.literal: If it is said that ruin comes by benevolence, that ruin is a worthy thing to buy even by a person selling himself.
ai.translation: If ruin is said to come from practicing benevolence, such ruin is worth acquiring even by selling oneself.
ai.modern: பிறருக்கு உதவி செய்வதனால் ஒருவனுக்கு அழிவு வரும் என்றால், அந்த அழிவை ஒருவன் தன்னை விற்றாவது வாங்கிக் கொள்ளும் தகுதி உடையதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet praises the supreme virtue of social benevolence (oppuravu). The poet states that even if helping others leads to one's own financial ruin or destruction, that ruin is not a loss to be feared. Instead, it is so glorious and noble that a person should be willing to sell themselves into slavery to purchase such a ruin. The words 'vittu' (selling) and 'kol' (buying) frame this ultimate sacrifice as a highly profitable moral transaction.
